content: 1. The effectiveness of the intervention could not be evaluated due to the presence of only a single study. 2. Additional data from a non-comparative descriptive analysis following the implementation of a Grindr-based outreach program revealed that 68% of Grindr contacts remained engaged after identifying the avatar as a health educator. Among these engaged contacts, 35% received a combination of services, including counseling, referrals, testing, treatment, and/or follow-up care. For those who self-identified for testing encounters, 14 individuals underwent testing for HIV, gonorrhea, and chlamydia, resulting in the identification of one case of pharyngeal chlamydia, two cases of rectal chlamydia, one case of urogenital chlamydia, and one new HIV infection. Additionally, 13 individuals were tested for syphilis, with one case of late latent syphilis identified. 3. A stepped-wedge cluster randomized controlled trial (RCT) conducted among 1,381 men who have sex with men (MSM) in China compared an integrated online HIV testing intervention (comprising a multimedia HIV testing campaign, an online HIV testing service, and local testing promotion campaigns tailored for MSM) to conventional HIV testing programs routinely provided by local Centers for Disease Control (CDC) and community-based organizations (CBOs). 4. The control group in the Tang 2018 study was based on baseline data from 1,318 participants, representing the standard of care. 5. Another RCT among 100 MSM in China compared online HIV self-testing via a private WeChat group (providing app-based messages and referrals to HIV services) to watching a brief instructional video on self-administering an oral HIV self-test kit. 6. The risk of bias in the above study was downgraded once due to detection bias. Blinding was not feasible given the nature of the intervention, and self-reported data may have been influenced by the lack of blinding. 7. The study also had a small sample size (≤50 participants in each arm), but no additional downgrading was applied for this limitation. 8. The adjusted risk ratio (RR) reported in the GRADE assessment was derived from the study authors' analysis, accounting for variables such as group, time, age, education, income, occupation, and household registration (hukou). 9. A meta-analysis used a model adjusted for age, marital status, and income. The Tang study also reported HIV testing outcomes in the past three months, disaggregated by age group (≤30 and >30 years old) and participation in in-person community activities. 10. Another RCT among 200 HIV-negative MSM and transgender women aged 15–19 in Thailand compared the use of a mobile app with youth-friendly services, PrEP self-assessment, rewards, and appointment reminders to youth-friendly services alone. 11. The risk of bias in this study was downgraded once due to concerns about randomization and allocation processes, which were not documented. Baseline differences in sociodemographic characteristics and outcome measures between groups suggested potential issues. 12. A cohort study among 238 HIV-positive adults soon to be released from prison in the USA compared an online tailored personalized website for HIV/STI testing to access an online provider directory webpage only. The study did not adjust for baseline and time-varying confounding factors. 13. Another cohort study among 120 HIV-positive MSM and transgender women aged 18–34 in the USA compared those who completed a six-month digital HIV care navigation intervention (text messaging with a personal HIV care navigator) to those who did not complete the intervention. Among the 120 participants, 60 were lost to follow-up, and the remaining 60 were considered the intervention group. The control group consisted of those lost to follow-up, with reasons including phone loss, relocation, or unknown causes. 14. An RCT among 90 HIV-positive stimulant-using MSM in the USA compared a mobile app intervention (APP+) with IMB HIV/ART content, a choose your own adventure story, and medication self-monitoring to no treatment. 15. Another RCT among 110 HIV-positive adults soon to be or recently released from prison in the USA compared the CARE+ Corrections intervention (computerized motivational interview and individual risk reduction plan pre-release, plus post-release text messaging for care navigation) to an attention-control group (opioid overdose prevention video and HIV provider/resource printout). 16. A cohort study among 1,201 HIV-positive prisoners in the USA compared those using telemedicine for HIV care to those receiving on-site management by correctional facility physicians. The control group consisted of prisoners who received standard on-site care before the implementation of telemedicine. 17. An RCT among 130 MSM in the USA compared a tailored website intervention (customized based on prior testing experiences, motivations, barriers, and resources) to access to an online provider directory with no tailored content. The intervention arm included 86 participants, while the control arm included 44 participants. 18. Another RCT among 112 MSM in the USA compared the use of social networks and peer leaders on Facebook to deliver HIV information in group settings and individually (via chat, wall posts, and personal messages) to peer leaders delivering general health information. 19. The intervention in the above study involved peer leaders disseminating health information tailored to participant responses and engagement through Facebook groups of 12 members. This was not strictly targeted health information as the tailoring was based on baseline assessment data collected during the study.
